newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says peace prospects up to Israel, PLO.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says peace prospects up to Israel, PLO.

text.p: The United States told Israel on Friday that it could provide only limited help to move the Middle East peace process forward, and it was up to the Israelis and Palestinians to make the compromises needed.

Secretary of State Madeleine Albright also made clear at a meeting with Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy that she was not prepared to visit the region until the parties made the "difficult decisions" required to break the current deadlock.

The meeting at the State Department came amid hints that Washington may trim its traditional hefty aid allocation to Israel and reassign funds to Jordan to reward King Hussein for his loyalty to the peace process.

Both Israel and the Palestinians have looked to Washington to resolve the impasse in their talks, stalled for two months over Israeli housing projects in Jerusalem and the West Bank which the PLO says violate previous accords.
"Obviously the United States will do what we can here and we'll keep pursuing our role, but it is the parties which have to make the difficult decisions," Albright told reporters before the meeting.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said Albright's "major point" to Levy was that while Washington wanted to bring the parties back to the table, "we cannot do that if they are not willing to make the appropriate efforts."
Albright told reporters she would go to the Middle East "when the time is ripe and when the parties are prepared to make some of the decisions that are really required."
U.S. Middle East envoy Dennis Ross has been touring the region this week. He was expected to fly back to Washington Friday night and report to President Bill Clinton and Albright, Burns said.
On aid to Jordan, Albright neither confirmed nor denied reports that an increased package could come out of Israel's annual allocation.
Israel Radio reported on Thursday that Ross had raised the issue of a possible $50 million cut in U.S. aid in talks with Israeli officials.
Albright said the United States had been looking for some time for ways to increase aid to Jordan "and the other friends of peace in the Middle East."
She said Clinton had discussed the issue with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who shared an interest in establishing what she called "a fund for Middle East peace and security".
"We are now examining with the Israelis details on how best to move forward on this, and when we reach a conclusion on this we'll be consulting with Congress," she said.

Levy said that "aid to Jordan is a mutual desire of the United States and Israel. It's an important link to strengthen the peace process. I'm sure we will find a common way in order to achieve this goal."

Israel receives about $3 billion annually from the United States and Egypt some $2 billion. Jordan received just $47 million in economic and military aid in 1997 and Clinton asked for $75.6 million in his 1998 budget request.
Burns said the aid being contemplated for Jordan would be in addition to that.

In Cairo, Palestinian President Yasser Arafat's spokesman Marwan Kanafani said on Friday the Middle East peace process was "clinically dead" and urged the United States to resurrect it. He said Arafat had sent a letter to Clinton saying the president must act quickly to save the process.
Burns said the "very negative statements" being made by some Palestinian officials were "not warranted".
